newsitem.title: HONG KONG: YEAREND-Red star of China rises over Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Red star of China rises over Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong's final year as a British colony was marked by farewells, shifting loyalties and hard-eyed jockeying for position as China tightened its grip and the balance of power shifted inexorably into Beijing's orbit.
Beijing crowned its ascendancy as 1996 drew to a close when it anointed its man to take the helm in mid-1997 when the British withdraw from their last major foreign outpost.

When the red flag of China flutters over Hong Kong next year, Tung Chee-hwa, a conservative Shanghai-born billionaire whose given names mean "Build China", will head this prosperous community of more than six million people.
Like so many families here, his shipowning family fled to Hong Kong ahead of the Chinese Communist takeover in 1949.

But as China prepares to right the humiliation of a foreign power occupying her soil and take Hong Kong back from the British at the stroke of midnight on June 30, 1997, old slights have been forgotten and new alliances forged.
Governor Chris Patten insisted his was not a lame-duck administration. While he would cooperate with Tung, he, Patten, would remain in charge until the handover.
"The British are no longer powerful," said independent pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau.
Hong Kong tycoons, assiduously wooed by Beijing, have been appointed to positions of power in transitional bodies alongside an old-guard of "friends of China".
Chinese companies rushed to list on the Hong Kong stock market and to invest in Hong Kong's sky-high property market.
SYMBOLS OF EMPIRE FADE
As China's star rose, the symbols of more than 150 years of empire faded. Queen Elizabeth's head disappeared from coins. The Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club, dropped its Royal prefix.
Gurkha infantry battalions marched into the sunset as the British garrison wound down in preparation for the handover.
The Royal Navy's patrol ships went up for auction. So did the Royal Air Force's fleet of ageing Wessex helicopters.
Prime Minister John Major made probably the last visit by a British leader before the handover, and promised Hong Kong would never walk alone.
"What would the British do?" asked Hong Kong stockbroker Alan Au. "Send warships? I think not."
It was a year when patriotic passion boiled over.
Occupation by Japanese rightists of a small island in an uninhabited chain called the Diaoyu in Chinese and Senkuku in Japanese and claimed by Beijing, Tokyo and Taipei, caused outrage.

Marchers took to the streets, picketed Japanese stores and in a moment of heady fervour stormed the Japanese consulate. Infuriated protesters chartered boats and attempted to dodge a Japanese flotilla in attempts to symbolically reclaim the islands for China. One voyage ended in grief when protester David Chan tried to swim ashore and drowned.
NOT ENTIRELY A CHINA HONEYMOON

But it was not all a honeymoon for China. Officials, particularly Beijing's official in charge of Hong Kong affairs Lu Ping, found themselves replacing British officials as targets of Hong Kong's energetic protesters.
Small but noisy demonstrations dogged Lu on each of his visits as protesters accused China of seeking to quash Hong Kong's freedoms and roll back democratic reforms.
More than 15,000 applicants, most of them China-born, kicked, elbowed and jostled their way queuing for British travel documents in March in a public show of concern over the future.
It was a bleak year for Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby which had benefited from the electoral reforms brought by Patten, the 28th and last British governor.

The Democracy Party, Hong Kong's biggest, marked the one year countdown with a candlelight vigil outside the Legislative Council building, greeting the stroke of midnight on 30 June 1996 with a chorus of "we shall overcome".

The democracy lobby expects to be kicked out of the Legislative Council when China replaces the chamber with an appointed provisional body in order to undo democratic reforms sponsored by Patten in the twilight of British rule.
Pro-democracy activists boycotted the China selection process which returned Tung as Chief Executive-designate and chose the provisional legislature, calling it a sham.

But there was no shortage of willing volunteers for the provisional chamber. More than 130 applications were lodged for 60 seats. About half of the existing legislature applied as did a handful of pro-China politicians defeated in the 1995 polls.
The trepidation about next year's handover felt by the pro-democracy lobby and those who rushed for passports was not shared by the business sector.
STOCK EXCHANGE AT DIZZY NEW HEIGHTS

Hong Kong's stock exchange soared to dizzy new heights in the last year of British rule. The blue chip index, the Hang Seng, added an impressive 30 percent in 1996 buoyed by money from overseas and particularly from China.
"The 1997 handover... has been totally discounted," Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp chief economist George Leung said.

Hong Kong's foreign currency reserves, described by a former British mandarin as the richest dowry since Cleopatra, mushroomed. Hong Kong had more than US$60 billion in the bank at the end of September.
Hong Kong's first locally-born Financial Secretary made part of his maiden budget speech in the local language, Cantonese, for the first time.

Donald Tsang, who faces the tricky prospect of drafting a budget which straddles the change of sovereignty, said he expected "a lot of shouting ahead" but insisted Hong Kong would remain fiscally autonomous with its own currency and economy.
Despite the uncertainty and fretting over freedom of speech, movement and assembly, Hong Kong remained a place where life is lived with earthy gusto and 25 hours is squeezed from every day.
When windsurfer Lee Lai-shan triumphed at the Olympic Games to bring home Hong Kong's first -- and possibly last -- gold medal, Hong Kong overflowed with joy.
The British colony mourned when 40 people perished in the worst fire to sweep through a high-rise building and when three schoolchildren and two teachers were killed in a freak bushfire.
If Hong Kong weathers the challenge, Patten and the business community, agreeing for once, predict it could be the golden city of Asia, the regional hub for finance, business and trade.
VINDICATION FOR DENG

That would be a vindication of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's vision. He took the risk of promising Hong Kong considerable autonomy under a one country, two systems policy designed also to woo Taiwan into the fold.
Deng said Hong Kong could maintain its freedoms and capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.

He is ailing now, but Hong Kong no longer responds to rumours about his health with the panic of the early 1980s when traders worried that hardliners in Beijing would seize power and send the bamboo curtain crashing down again.
The reforms have gone too far to be reversed, they say, and Hong Kong will continue to prosper from China's economic boom.
If anything, Hong Kong optimists say, the China of the 21st century is more likely to resemble the Hong Kong of today.
The pessimists respond that the jury remains out.
